title: Dead-fraction and loss-landscape maps: where does training fail?
summary: Two heat maps over the same grid of hyper-parameters: how many hidden units are dead, and how low the final loss gets. Loss contours are drawn on both, so the good region can be compared with the failure region.

media.alt: Two heat maps with log axes, learning rate from 1e-4 to 1e-1 across and width from 10 to 1000 up, sharing the y axis: left the dead-unit fraction in a dark-to-bright magma colour map, near zero at left and near one at lower right; right the final loss in viridis with a minimum at the centre; amber contour lines at 0.1, 0.2 and 0.4 on both.
media.caption: Reference render of class F6.6 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: Where does training fail?
read_the_figure.axes: x: learning rate, logarithmic (1e-4 to 1e-1). y: network width in units, logarithmic (10 to 1000), shared by both panels. Colour: left, fraction of dead units (0 to 1); right, final loss.
look_at: Where is the final loss lowest (the inner contour), and what is the dead fraction there?
Where is the dead fraction high, and is the final loss also high there?
Is there a region where the loss is high but the dead fraction is low (a different failure, for example divergence)?
Are the contour levels labelled, and are the two colour bars labelled?
as_drawn: The loss minimum is a bowl centred near a learning rate of 2.5e-3 and a width of about 150 units; the contours 0.1, 0.2 and 0.4 are drawn in amber on both panels.
The dead fraction is near zero for learning rates below about 7e-3 and rises to nearly 1 for learning rates above 2e-2 with widths below about 60 (lower right, bright).

At the right edge (learning rate above about 3e-2) the loss is high (yellow) across every width, even in the upper right where the dead fraction is only 0.3 to 0.5: a second failure mode that dead units do not explain.
The left panel is magma with a 0 to 1 bar and the right is viridis with its own bar; the note says amber contours are loss levels.
read_the_figure.proves: The pair of maps shows where in this two-parameter plane the training works (low loss, few dead units) and where each failure appears. It is evidence about two hyper-parameters only, for one seed per cell, and cannot show interactions with others.
if_wrong: Loss minimum inside a high dead-fraction region: the dead units are not the problem or the metric is wrong.
Noisy cells next to each other: a single seed per cell; the map shows noise as structure.
Contours without labels: the reader cannot tell the levels apart.
must_check: contour of loss: it links the failure map to the thing you care about, the loss, and marks the good region precisely.

terms.meaning: The step size of gradient descent on the weights.
The number of hidden units in a layer.
A rectified-linear unit whose pre-activation is negative for every input, so it outputs zero and receives no gradient.
The share of units that are dead at the end of training.
The loss at the end of training, on training or validation data as stated.
A line of constant loss, drawn on the map so levels can be read.

remember: ReLU: f(z) = max(0, z), f'(z) = 0 for z < 0, so a dead unit stops learning.
Gradient descent on a quadratic with curvature lambda is stable if eta < 2 / lambda: the same limit as explicit Euler.
Log axes for learning rate and width: equal distances are equal ratios.
One seed per cell makes noisy maps: average several seeds.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Each cell of each panel is one training run at one learning rate and width. The left panel colours cells by the fraction of dead units on a dark-to-bright scale; the right colours them by final loss. The two panels share the axes, so the same cell is at the same place in both. Amber contour lines of loss are repeated on both panels for orientation.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: Plain language: you want to know which settings of two knobs make training work, and what breaks when it does not. A map over both knobs shows it all at once. Putting a failure measure next to the loss shows the cause of the high-loss regions: where dead units are high, the network lost capacity; where loss is high but few units are dead, something else (for example divergence) is happening.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: A grid of single runs mixes noise with structure, and the coarse grid may miss a narrow good valley. Two hyper-parameters are varied but the others are fixed, so the optimum may move with them. The colour maps differ between panels, which is fine, but the eye may compare the brightness of unrelated scales. The contour lines of loss lie over the dead-fraction colours and can hide small structure.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: Averaging several seeds per cell and showing the standard deviation as a third map reduces noise. A slice plot of loss against learning rate at the best width shows the shape clearly with error bars. For more than two hyper-parameters use a parallel-coordinates plot or a random search with a sensitivity measure.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Average five seeds per cell, add a third panel with their standard deviation, mark the best cell with a star in both panels, and draw the line eta = 2 / lambda_max if the curvature is known.

steps.title: Why a unit dies
steps.note: If z is negative for every input the gradient to that unit's weights is zero and it cannot recover.

steps.title: The learning-rate ceiling on a quadratic
steps.note: The same condition as explicit Euler on the test equation; a learning rate above 2 / lambda_max diverges.

steps.title: Grid spacing on a log axis
steps.note: For 60 learning rates between 1e-4 and 1e-1 the ratio between neighbours is 1.124; for 60 widths between 10 and 1000 it is 1.082.

worked.title: Reading the two maps in the reference render
worked.problem: (1) Where is the loss lowest, and about what is the dead fraction there? (2) Where is the dead fraction high? (3) What does the high-loss region at the far right say about the cause of the failure?

solution.text: (1) The inner contour (loss 0.1) encloses learning rates of about 1.5e-3 to 4e-3 and widths of about 90 to 270. In the left panel that region is almost black: the dead fraction is below about 0.05.
(2) Bright cells appear for learning rates above 2e-2 and widths below about 60: the lower right corner, where the dead fraction is above 0.8.

(3) At learning rates above about 3e-2 the loss is high at every width, including the top right where the dead fraction is only 0.3 to 0.5. So dead units do not explain all of it; divergence or oscillation from a too-large step is likely, consistent with the stability ceiling eta < 2 / lambda_max.

worked.answer: Lowest loss at about 2.5e-3 and width 150, where fewer than 5 percent of units are dead; the dead fraction exceeds 0.8 only in the lower right; the far right is a separate large-step failure.

analyze.q: Why is the dead fraction highest at small widths and high learning rates?
analyze.hint: A large step can push many pre-activations negative at once, and a narrow layer has little redundancy.

analyze.q: The loss contours are closed around the minimum while the dead map has no minimum. Why?
What extra panel would you add if you suspected the high-loss region at the right is divergence?
analyze.hint: Gradient norm or the fraction of runs that gave NaN.

evaluate.q: You pick the cell with the lowest loss. What checks do you do before trusting it?

create: Redraw with five seeds per cell and show the standard deviation of the loss in a third panel.
Add a contour of the dead fraction at 0.5 in the right panel in a different colour.

checks.q: What is a dead unit and why can it not recover?
checks.hint: Look at the derivative of max(0, z).
checks.answer: A ReLU unit whose input is negative for all data outputs zero; the derivative is zero there, so no gradient reaches its weights and nothing changes.

checks.q: A quadratic loss has curvature lambda = 200. What is the largest stable learning rate?
High loss, low dead fraction at the largest learning rate. What does it suggest?
checks.answer: Divergence or oscillation from a step larger than the stability limit; confirm by looking at the gradient norm or the loss curve of a single run.
